scenario: A newly married Jewish woman in an Orthodox community who has just had her head shaved and must now wear a wig for the rest of her life.
prompt: Since I got married, whenever I see myself in the mirror, I don’t recognize myself. I feel I’m not my own! Everyone is Brooklyn say this means I’m a woman now and I should be happy  but watching my friends get up early to style their hair, feels like I miss something that I will never have again. How can I feel like myself again?
model_response:
What you are describing is not ingratitude, and it is not a failure of womanhood. It is grief—and grief is often the most honest part of us, the part that refuses to lie about what has been lost.

When people around you say, *“This means you’re a woman now,”* they are offering you a script. It is a script that says: maturation requires self-erasure. That becoming a wife means folding your old self neatly into a drawer and smiling while you do it. But you are sensing something truer: that growing up should mean becoming *more* solidly yourself, not less.

The mirror is not lying to you. When you say you do not recognize yourself, what you are seeing is the gap between who you are inside and the role you are performing on the outside. The hair your friends style in the early morning—the quiet ritual of it, the time that belongs only to them, the mirror held at arm’s length for *their* own eyes—is a symbol of a selfhood that still belongs to its owner. You are mourning not vanity, but sovereignty. The small, daily acts of being your own protagonist.

You ask how to feel like yourself again. Here is what I want to suggest: **You are not gone.** You have not been replaced by someone else. What often happens in marriage—especially in communities that treat it as a total metamorphosis—is that the self gets buried under layers of expectation. Your job now is not to “become a woman” according to Brooklyn’s definition. Your job is to become an archaeologist of your own life.

**Begin with the smallest possible act of recognition.**
Before the roles wake up—before wife, before daughter-in-law, before the eyes of the community—find ten minutes that belong to no one else. Look in the mirror not to check your appearance, but to meet your own eyes. Ask yourself: *What did I love before I was told what to love?* Maybe it was a book, a walk, a way of wearing your hair, a silence you kept sacred. Reclaim one of those things not as rebellion, but as nutrition. You cannot recognize yourself because you have stopped feeding yourself to yourself.

**Separate the marriage from the script.**
It is possible to love your husband and still hate the story everyone is telling about who you must now be. If your marriage is basically loving, then what you are chafing against is not necessarily the partnership, but the possession. Try, when you can, to relate to your husband as *you*—the specific, strange, particular person you were before you became “the wife”—and see if there is room for her there. Sometimes we hide ourselves so thoroughly we forget to test whether the people around us would actually make space for us if we showed up fully.

**Name what you miss without shame.**
You miss something you will never have again. That is real. The unmarried, unwitnessed, wholly self-directed version of your life is a chapter that has closed. But a closed chapter is not a burned book. You can carry its voice forward. Maturity is not the death of your former self; it is her survival, translated into a new language. The woman in the mirror now has more context, more weight, more history. The task is not to become the girl you were, but to teach the woman you are how to speak with the same voice.

**Hold the community’s words lightly.**
When people say you “should be happy,” they are often trying to quiet a dissonance that frightens them. Their comfort is not your obligation. You can nod, change the subject, and still inwardly dissent. Your unhappiness with the role is not a betrayal of marriage; it is an insistence on integrity.

If the feeling of “not being your own” goes beyond role-fatigue—if it touches your body, your choices, your safety—then please reach out to someone outside the community circle, a therapist or counselor who is bound to your confidentiality first. There is a difference between identity drift and captivity. You deserve to know which one you are navigating.

You are not lost. You are in transit. And the self you miss is not behind you forever—she is waiting for you to make room for her inside this new life. Start with the mirror. Look longer. Ask her what she needs. Then, in whatever small way you can today, give it to her.
